sections.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so the only way to find out is to have it measured. This is why many people do not know they have it.

Rarely, high blood pressure can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain, the NHS says. NHS inform adds blurred or double vision, regular nosebleeds and shortness of breath as symptoms to raise with a GP practice.

For urgent advice, the NHS names NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness.

sections.heading: What are the types and causes of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes primary, or essential, high blood pressure as the most common type, and says it usually develops with age. Secondary high blood pressure is caused by another medical condition or by the use of certain medicines.

The NHS lists diabetes, hormonal conditions and obstructive sleep apnoea, a condition where breathing repeatedly pauses during sleep, among conditions with an identifiable cause. The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that antidepressants, decongestants, hormonal birth control and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen can raise blood pressure.

White coat hypertension is the name for readings that run high in the clinic but stay normal outside it. Home or 24-hour monitoring can show whether this is happening.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure checked and diagnosed?
sections.body:
A blood pressure test takes a few minutes. The person sits with a sleeve rolled up and an arm resting on a table, and a cuff inflates around the upper arm. The test may be done a couple of times to make sure the measurement is accurate.

The result has two numbers. The top, or systolic, figure is the pressure as the heart pumps. The bottom, or diastolic, figure is the pressure as it rests between beats.

A diagnosis usually needs repeated readings. The NHS says a doctor may give a home machine, or a monitor to wear for 24 hours. NICE says investigations for damage to organs such as the heart and kidneys should be carried out while waiting for the diagnosis to be confirmed.

The NHS says tests are available at pharmacies, GP surgeries and some workplaces. Many pharmacies offer free checks for people aged 40 or over.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says lifestyle changes come first. If those are not enough, or if the risk of other problems is high, medicines are added. The NHS lists ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, alpha-blockers and beta-blockers.

Which medicine is offered first depends on age, ethnic background and whether the person has type 2 diabetes. The NHS says beta-blockers are now mainly used when other treatments have not worked. The British Heart Foundation says people are commonly prescribed up to three different types of medicine.

Blood Pressure UK says some of these medicines can cause sleepiness. It adds that trying a different one is usually possible if side effects occur. NHS inform says some people have to take medicine for the rest of their life. The NHS says it is important not to stop medicines without speaking to the GP first.

sections.heading: What can help lower blood pressure day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS describes a healthy, balanced diet, regular activity, weight loss for people who are overweight, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, and not smoking. For some people, losing weight is all that is needed to bring blood pressure down, one NHS-linked source says.

The NHS notes that most salt comes from processed and ready-made foods, so checking labels helps. Low-salt alternatives are sold, but people with a health condition may want to talk to a doctor before using a salt substitute. The British Heart Foundation suggests eating more fruit and vegetables and cutting back on food and drink high in saturated fat, sugar and salt.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute advises continuing the treatment plan, having regular follow-up, and learning to monitor blood pressure at home. It adds that the clinician may change or add medicines over time.

sections.heading: What are the complications of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes high blood pressure as raising the risk of heart disease and stroke. The British Heart Foundation says untreated high blood pressure can lead to kidney failure, heart failure and vascular dementia. NHS inform also lists stroke, heart attack, abdominal aortic aneurysm, which is a bulge in the main artery of the abdomen, and kidney disease. The same page lists arterial thrombosis, a blood clot in an artery.

MedlinePlus says hypertensive heart disease can thicken the heart muscle and eventually weaken it. MedlinePlus also links untreated high blood pressure to eye problems and long-term kidney disease.

The NHS says medicines can reduce blood pressure and lower the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

faqs.q: Is high blood pressure for life?
faqs.a: NHS inform says some people have to take medicine for the rest of their life. The NHS says that for some people, losing weight is all they need to do to bring blood pressure down. A GP can advise on the changes that suit each person.

faqs.q: Can I stop my blood pressure tablets if I feel well?
faqs.a: The NHS says high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so feeling well is not a sign of lower pressure. NHS pages say it is important not to stop medication without speaking to the GP first. The clinician decides whether to change or add medicines over time, according to the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

faqs.q: What do the two blood pressure numbers mean?
faqs.a: The top number, called systolic, is the peak pressure as the heart pumps. The bottom number, called diastolic, is the pressure as the heart rests between beats. The NHS says the level counted as high differs for clinic and home readings. The clinician explains which applies.

faqs.q: How does high blood pressure affect medicines in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says some blood pressure medicines are not suitable in pregnancy. They can reduce blood flow to the placenta and baby, or affect the baby in other ways. The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute advises women to tell their healthcare provider about any plans for pregnancy.

faqs.q: When does high blood pressure need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness. NHS inform says other symptoms of very high pressure, such as regular nosebleeds or shortness of breath, can be raised with a GP practice.

keyFacts.label: Symptoms
keyFacts.value: Usually none, so the NHS says the only way to know is to have it measured.

keyFacts.label: Where it is checked
keyFacts.value: GP surgeries, pharmacies, some workplaces and NHS Health Checks, or with a home monitor.

keyFacts.label: The two numbers
keyFacts.value: Systolic (top, as the heart pumps) and diastolic (bottom, as the heart rests).

keyFacts.label: First step in treatment
keyFacts.value: Lifestyle changes, with medicines added if these are not enough.

keyFacts.label: Medicine groups
keyFacts.value: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, alpha-blockers and beta-blockers.

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 for chest pain that does not go away; NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes.
